text: The pages for March are water-stained, and the figures on them have been copied out again on the facing page in a much neater hand. Whoever made the copy also changed three of the totals.
strengths: the visible detail leads straight to evidence
the second sentence turns a description into a discovery
weaknesses: the stains and the neat hand are what the shot of the ledger already shows
spokenRhythm: A long descriptive sentence followed by a shorter one that carries the finding.
narrativeFunction: Uses the condition of a document to introduce a discrepancy in it.
whyItWorks: Naming a visible feature is acceptable when the feature is the clue. Here the stains suggest why the page was copied, and the copy is where the totals changed, so the description earns its place by leading to a fact the picture cannot show.
whyItFails: If the narration names what is visible on every document, it becomes a voice describing the screen. Water stains and a neater hand are the camera's job unless they matter to the argument. Keep this once, where the physical state of the source is the evidence, and use the plainer version everywhere else.
rewrite: The figures for March were copied out a second time on the facing page. Whoever made the copy changed three of the totals.

text: No drawing of the first camp survives. The surveyor's letters describe a row of tents on a gravel bar, a cook-house roofed with an old sail, and a flagpole with no flag. Within a month, the river had taken all of it.
strengths: says plainly that no image exists before describing anything
every visual detail is credited to the letters
the description ends on an event rather than on mood
weaknesses: three visual details in one breath is the most a listener can take
the flagpole with no flag is chosen for charm as much as for information
spokenRhythm: A short statement of absence, a long sentence of three sourced details, and a short close that sweeps them away.
narrativeFunction: Gives the audience a picture of a place the film has no picture of, then moves the story on.
whyItWorks: When nothing survives to show, describing the place is the narration's job rather than a duplicate of the picture's. Naming the letters keeps the description on the record instead of in the writer's imagination, and it stops after three plain details.
whyItFails: It fails the moment the film cuts to a painting or a reconstruction of the camp, because the narration is then describing the screen. It also tempts the writer past the letters into smoke, weather and faces that nobody recorded. Use it only where the absence of a picture is real, keep to what the source says, and keep it short.

text: It is the third day of the festival, and the grain ships from the south have not come in. The city's granaries hold enough for perhaps ten days. The magistrates have already promised the crowd a free distribution at the end of the week.
strengths: puts the listener inside a single day without telling them to imagine it
each sentence adds a stake rather than a sight
the hedge on the granaries survives the switch to the present tense
weaknesses: the present tense claims a vantage on one particular day that the record may only partly support
spokenRhythm: A long opening that sets the day, a short line for the stocks, and a medium close that adds the promise.
narrativeFunction: Opens a scene of waiting by stating the shortfall and the promise that makes the waiting dangerous.
whyItWorks: The historic present can set a scene briskly, the way someone telling a story at a table slips into it. Here it is filled with stocks, days and a promise rather than with weather and faces, so it does what an imagine opener tries to do without the command.
whyItFails: Present tense pulls writers toward describing what is seen, the crowd in the square or the light on the harbour, and over a whole film it starts to sound like a trailer. It also blurs reconstruction and record. Use it to open one scene, then return to the past tense when the narration turns to evidence.
rewrite: On the third day of the festival, the grain ships from the south had still not come in. The city's granaries held enough for perhaps ten days, and the magistrates had already promised the crowd a free distribution at the end of the week.
